title: CTDP1 governs a Pol II phosphorylation intermediate and coordinates Mediator recruitment; transcription efficiency; and splicing.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and parsed three files: the GEO RNA-seq count table GSE312502_RNA-seq_counts_for_GEO.xlsx (15,149 Ensembl mouse genes x 10 columns = 5 time points x 2 replicates of catalytically dead CTDP1 induction, spike-in normalised, 0 duplicate gene identifiers, 0 missing cells; replicate agreement of the 48 h vs 0 h log2 change on 13,429 expressed genes was Pearson 0.91); the PRIDE phosphoproteomics export ZHN_20250526_phos-WT-MT.xlsx, which I de-nested into 2,902 protein rows and 12,204 phospho-peptide rows (9,047 unique peptide sequences, 2,932 master proteins, 10,408 distinct phospho-sites as UniProt accession + residue position, 10,603 rows carrying the 'Abundance Ratio: (DOX)/(UN)' label, 7,565 rows with all six replicate intensities, median within-condition replicate standard deviation 0.19-0.22 in log2 units); and the PRIDE immunoprecipitation table ZHN_20250425_RPB1ChIP-WT-MT.xlsx (2,668 protein rows with a mutant/wild-type abundance ratio). I also listed both GEO series by FTP: GSE223475 holds only a 15 GB raw archive plus ~100 bigWig coverage tracks of 60-400 MB each and four .hic files of ~0.5 GB; GSE312502 holds a 6.4 GB raw archive, 34 bigWig tracks and the one count table. PRIDE holds 13 files, of which the large ones are raw mass-spectrometry archives (3-9 GB).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That alternative splicing was quantified with rMATS v4.1.2 and that Supplementary Table S3 lists only the number of differential splicing events (no per-event table is deposited anywhere I could reach); that three candidate sites on the splicing factors RBM14, YTHDC1 and BCLF1 were confirmed by in vitro dephosphorylation of synthetic peptides; that phospho-peptides with two or more missing replicate values were discarded before the paper's own statistics (the deposited export is unfiltered). The journal's supplementary archive was not retrievable - the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint timed out twice at 120 s, so Supplementary Tables S1-S4 were never opened.

a1_downloadable.note: Verified: three files downloaded anonymously over HTTPS from the PRIDE and GEO FTP mirrors; no login, no access application.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the phospho-site task the label is literally a column I read ('Abundance Ratio: (DOX)/(UN)', present for 10,603 of 12,204 peptide rows). Caveat: the paper's more interesting outcomes (intron retention, Mediator and Pol II occupancy) are NOT deposited as tables and would have to be rebuilt from 22 GB of raw reads or from bigWig coverage tracks.

a3_inputs_present.note: Verified: each row carries the annotated peptide sequence (e.g. '[R].SRSRASPATHR.[R]') plus site positions on a UniProt accession ('Q8BTI8 3xPhospho [S1820(100); S1822(100)...]'), so no identifier hunting is needed for the local sequence window.

a4_units_stated.note: Marginal pass checked in the file: the label is a dimensionless abundance ratio and the six intensity columns are arbitrary mass-spectrometry intensities that the methods say were normalised to each sample's library size. The file itself carries no units row and no data dictionary.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified by counting: 10,603 phospho-peptide rows with a label, covering 10,408 distinct sites on 2,932 proteins. The experiment behind them, however, is a single three-versus-three comparison.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~20 MB (2.5 MB phospho export + 0.3 MB immunoprecipitation export + 2.1 MB count table + a mouse reference proteome)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Verified file sizes; everything used fits in a few hundred megabytes of RAM. The raw archives and coverage tracks (22 GB total) are deliberately not used.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Nothing disagrees, because the paper states no phospho-peptide, phospho-site or gene count at all (the only count I could find in the text was '249 genes'). The deposited export is the unfiltered search output; the paper's filtered list is not deposited.

a8_label_provenance.note: The label is a measured label-free intensity ratio from an Orbitrap instrument, not another model's output, and site positions come from search-engine localisation scores shown as percentages. Important caveat, not a technical failure: the measurement is the response to over-expressing a catalytically dead CTDP1, which mixes direct dephosphorylation targets with large indirect effects (the same perturbation shuts down global transcription, as the count table shows).

B1.why: One file, but a nested Proteome Discoverer export: protein rows interleaved with peptide blocks, de-nested by my own script.

B2.why: Opens in pandas but the real header sits on row 3 and peptide blocks repeat headers; needed custom parsing.

B3.why: Single run, label-free ratio already library-size normalised by the authors; verified columns in the file.

B4.why: 1,601 of 12,204 peptide rows lack a ratio and only 7,565 have all six intensities; missing, easy to drop.

B5.why: 12,204 rows but 9,047 unique peptides and 10,408 sites, so a site-collapse rule is needed; counted in the file.

B6.why: Standard software column names, but file name says WT-MT while columns say DOX/UN; no data dictionary.

C1.why: A failure to predict site responses could equally mean label noise, indirect effects, or no sequence signal.

C2.why: No model of CTDP1 specificity found, but DephosSite and kinase-substrate models cover the adjacent task; searched.

C3.why: Nobody has modelled phosphatase-perturbation responses here, but one indirect perturbation weakens the angle.

C4.why: Finding phosphatase substrates today needs immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry plus in vitro assays, per the paper's own methods.

C5.why: Obvious dummies exist (per-protein mean, proline-directed motif rule); no published number for this task.

D1.why: ESM-2, an open-weight protein language model, directly fits 31-residue sequence windows around each site.

D2.why: About 10,000 short windows embed once on a laptop CPU in well under an hour; no fine-tuning needed.

D3.why: ESM-2 weights are MIT licensed; the data files are public GEO and PRIDE deposits.

E1.why: Grouped split by master protein accession (2,932 groups) or by sequence-similarity cluster; accession column seen in file.

E2.why: 2,932 master proteins verified in the parsed table, far more than the five groups needed.

E3.why: Global mean and per-protein mean of the log2 ratio are computable directly from the parsed columns.

E4.why: Three replicates per condition; I measured median within-condition log2 standard deviation of 0.19-0.22.

E5.why: Pol II C-terminal domain Ser2/Ser5 sites plus RBM14, YTHDC1 and BCLF1 sites validated in vitro must rank high.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature ablation are trivial on a 10,603-row table.

E7.why: No second phosphatase-perturbation phospho-proteome joins off the shelf; no year or source column in the file.

E8.why: Paper publishes no predictive number, and its own filtered differential list is not deposited, so nothing to reproduce.

G1.why: UniProt accessions plus exact residue positions are present in the 'Modifications in Master Proteins' column I parsed.

G2.why: PhosphoSitePlus and EPSD (phospho-site annotation) and the Johnson kinase-motif atlas all join on UniProt accession plus position.

G3.why: Accession-plus-position joins cleanly, but mouse site coverage in human-centric resources is patchy and needs orthology mapping.

G4.why: Asking which kinase motif classes this phosphatase counteracts is interesting but answerable by enrichment without a model.

H1.why: All quantified peptides are reported, responders and non-responders alike; 1,633 of 10,603 exceed twofold change.

H2.why: One lab, one mouse embryonic stem cell line, one instrument, one perturbation; verified from file names and methods.

H3.why: The honest claim can be written in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Methods describe the design, but the deposited file's DOX/UN labelling versus the paper's WT/MT framing is unexplained.

I1.why: Transcription-cycle and phosphatase-biology labs would read it; no named group is waiting for the prediction.

I2.why: A ranked candidate list could guide a few in vitro dephosphorylation assays; it would not redirect a programme.

I3.why: Precision among top-ranked sites matches the assay decision, but the label measures indirect response, not substrate status.

I4.why: Risk that per-protein mean or a simple proline-directed motif rule captures most variance; untested.

J1.why: Frozen protein language model embeddings, grouped splits, calibration: the modelling skills I want to practise.

J2.why: I can sanity-check phospho-motif results roughly, but judging CTDP1 substrate plausibility needs an expert.

J3.why: The de-nested site-level table with replicate noise estimates is a shareable artefact even if the model fails.

J4.why: Two weeks would plausibly cover it, but no budget is written down anywhere.

J5.why: A kill condition is easy to state (per-protein mean not beaten) but is not committed in NOTES.md.

existing_models.name: DephosSite (MGPS-DEPHOS and CKSAAP-DEPHOS, Scientific Reports 2016)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported as support-vector-machine predictors of phosphatase-specific dephosphorylation sites, trained mainly on tyrosine phosphatase substrate sites; evaluated by cross-validation on curated site lists, not on a held-out perturbation experiment.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Coverage of serine/threonine phosphatases and of individual phosphatase specificity beyond a handful of curated enzymes.

existing_models.name: SnapKin (NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics 2023), an ensemble deep-learning method for kinase-substrate prediction from phospho-proteomics data
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported to outperform earlier kinase-substrate predictors on benchmark phospho-proteomics datasets; evaluation is per-kinase cross-validation, not a grouped protein split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Extending the framework to phosphatases, which lack labelled substrate sets.

existing_models.name: CoPheeMap / CoPheeKSA (Nature Communications 2025), machine-learned co-regulation of phospho-sites across 1,195 tumours
existing_models.score_and_split: Reports 24,015 predicted associations between 9,399 phospho-sites and 104 serine/threonine kinases; validated against curated kinase-substrate databases.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Phosphatase-substrate relationships are explicitly named as missing from the co-regulation map for want of data.

existing_models.name: FuncPhos-SEQ (Cell Reports 2023), a sequence-plus-network deep model for phospho-site functional importance
existing_models.score_and_split: Predicts functional relevance of human phospho-sites from sequence motifs and protein-interaction embeddings; benchmarked on curated functional site annotations.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Transfer to non-human proteomes and to context-specific regulation.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (esm2_t33_650M or the smaller t12_35M), a protein language model
backbone.hardware: 16 GB laptop CPU; roughly 10,000 windows of 31 residues embed in well under an hour

integration.partner_dataset: PhosphoSitePlus and EPSD phospho-site annotation, plus the Johnson et al. kinase motif atlas
integration.join_key: UniProt accession + residue position (both present in the parsed export)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Which kinase motif classes does this Pol II phosphatase counteract, and are its responsive sites the same ones annotated as functional elsewhere?

controls.positive_control: Pol II C-terminal domain phospho-Ser2 and phospho-Ser5 sites, and the three splicing-factor sites (RBM14, YTHDC1, BCLF1) that the paper confirmed by in vitro dephosphorylation, must rank among the top predicted responders; plus a plumbing check of predicting peptide mass from sequence.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the log2 ratio labels within protein groups and confirm performance collapses to the per-protein mean; ablate the sequence window to leave only protein identity.
controls.external_validation: None available off the shelf: no second phosphatase-perturbation phospho-proteome in the same units, and no publication-year or source column for a temporal split.

honest_claim_h3: A model trained here could only claim to predict which phospho-peptides, among those detectable in one mouse embryonic stem cell mass-spectrometry run, change abundance when a catalytically dead version of CTDP1 is over-expressed for a single time point - which mixes direct dephosphorylation targets with the indirect consequences of a near-global transcription shutdown.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use the sequence around a phosphorylation site to predict whether it changes when a Pol II phosphatase is disabled
plain_idea.train_on: A 31-residue sequence window centred on each phosphorylated serine, threonine or tyrosine, plus simple context features; 10,603 measured phospho-peptides covering 10,408 distinct sites on 2,932 mouse proteins, counted in the deposited file.
plain_idea.predict: The log2 ratio of phospho-peptide abundance with versus without induction of a catalytically dead CTDP1, measured by label-free mass spectrometry on an Orbitrap instrument with three replicates per condition.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Phosphatase specificity rules are far less mapped than kinase ones, so a ranked candidate list could tell transcription-cycle labs which sites to test in vitro; even a failure would quantify how little sequence alone explains phosphatase perturbation responses.

more_or_better_data.why: 10,603 labelled peptides from a single three-versus-three comparison is small beside the datasets behind the named models (CoPheeKSA used 1,195 tumour phospho-proteomes; SnapKin was built on multiple published perturbation series), and it covers only one cell line.

confidence_score.why: Three replicates per condition give a real noise estimate (median within-condition log2 standard deviation 0.19-0.22, which I measured), so per-site uncertainty is computable; but with one experiment there is no way to separate measurement noise from biological variability across contexts.

models_beatable.why: DephosSite is a 2016 support-vector machine for tyrosine phosphatases with no usable weights, so it is weak, but it predicts a different quantity, so beating it would not be a like-for-like comparison; the strong 2023-2025 kinase models do not address this task at all.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No new data measures the same quantity the same way: there is no second CTDP1 perturbation phospho-proteome to add, and the existing models cannot be run as a baseline on this label, so the same-split, same-measurement conditions both fail.

ml_idea: De-nest the deposited Proteome Discoverer phospho-proteomics export into a site-level table (10,408 sites, 2,932 proteins), build 31-residue windows from the mouse reference proteome, embed them with frozen ESM-2, and predict the measured log2 change in phospho-peptide abundance upon induction of catalytically dead CTDP1, with a protein-grouped split, a per-protein-mean dummy baseline, and the validated RBM14/YTHDC1/BCLF1 and Pol II C-terminal domain sites as positive controls. The richer labels the paper actually cares about (intron retention, Mediator and Pol II occupancy) are not deposited in table form and would require reprocessing 22 GB of raw sequencing data.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from files I actually opened: the three tables total 5 MB and parsed in seconds on this laptop; the embedding figure assumes roughly 10,000 windows of 31 residues through ESM-2 650M on CPU at a few windows per second, which I did not time.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Fit the per-protein mean of the log2 ratio and measure how much variance is left: if protein identity alone explains most of it, a sequence model adds nothing and the project is dead in an afternoon.

verdict_reason: Part A passes on the files - the phospho-proteomics export really does contain 10,603 labelled phospho-peptides with sequences, site positions and replicate intensities, all in 2.5 MB - but the question is thin. The only modellable label is one three-versus-three mass-spectrometry comparison in a single mouse embryonic stem cell line, and it measures the indirect response to over-expressing a catalytically dead phosphatase (the same perturbation collapses global transcription, visible as a mean log2 change of -1.12 in the count table), not direct substrate status. Model-readiness scores 7 of 12 because the export is a nested software dump needing custom de-nesting and site collapse, there is no external validation set and no published number to reproduce, coverage is one lab and one cell type, and the per-protein mean may well explain most of the signal. The labels the paper's biology actually turns on - intron retention and Pol II or Mediator occupancy - were never deposited as tables; rebuilding them means reprocessing 22 GB of raw reads and roughly 130 coverage tracks, which is a different and much larger project.
